rubric: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS / GRAPHS AND PROBABILITY / CHAPTER 8

slides.title: Graphs: the basics
slides.main: The element tree, dependencies and a social network are graphs, even when they aren't called that.

captions: Graphs: the basics
The element tree in the developer tools is a graph
A project's dependencies are a graph too, however strange the word "tree" sounds
Friends, subscriptions, recommendations in a social network — graphs again
Today we speak about them strictly: vertices and edges, memory, the sum of degrees
This is the foundation for the next two chapters — there we will learn to walk along graphs

body.text: Today we learn to speak about links strictly, and in the next two chapters — to walk along graphs.

slides.title: What a graph is
slides.sub: A set of vertices and a set of edges
slides.main: No coordinates, no scale — only objects and the links between them.

captions: The definition will surprise you with its simplicity
A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges, where each edge connects a pair of vertices
No coordinates, no scale, no pretty lines — only objects and links
A map of friends: vertices are people, edges are friendship
A metro map: vertices are stations, edges are the stretches between them; arc or broken line — it doesn't matter

frames.text: V = {A,B,C,D,E}   E = {AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, BD}
the same graph — a different drawing

body.text: For a graph only the connection "this station is connected to that one" matters: a metro map and a list of stretches are the same graph.

slides.title: Direction of edges
slides.sub: The first design decision: arrows or not
slides.main: Mix up the type of graph and the algorithm will answer the wrong questions.

captions: The first question for any links is whether they are symmetric
Friendship is mutual: if I am your friend, you are mine — an undirected edge
A subscription is not mutual: I read a blogger, they don't notice me — a directed edge, an arrow
Links between pages, data flows, navigation around a site — all of these are arrows
The type of graph is the first design decision: mix it up and the algorithm answers the wrong questions

frames.text: different models — different questions and answers

body.text: Links between pages, data flows, navigation around a site — all of these are arrows.

slides.title: The handshake lemma
slides.sub: deg(v) — how many edges touch the vertex
slides.main: Each handshake adds one to both participants — in the sum of degrees each edge is counted twice.

captions: Every vertex has a degree: the number of edges that enter it
A popular one in a friendship graph has a large degree, a recluse has one or zero
The handshake lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges
The reason: each edge touches two vertices, and by summing degrees we count it twice
Consequence: the number of vertices of odd degree in any graph is even

frames.text: each edge contributes +1 to two vertices
odd vertices: 2 (E and F) — an even number

body.text: A non-obvious consequence: the number of vertices with an odd degree in any graph is even — here there are two. Such conclusions from simple counting are the signature flavor of graph theory.

slides.title: Paths and cycles
slides.main: "Is the database reachable from this service?" is a question about the existence of a path.

captions: Next — movement along a graph
A path is a sequence of vertices where each next one is connected to the previous by an edge: home → shop → work
The length of a path is the number of edges in it
A cycle is a path returning to the starting vertex without repeating edges: a circular route around the neighborhood
Problems like "is the database reachable from this service" rest on the existence of a path

frames.text: home → shop → café → home: a cycle
path service → API → DB: DB reachable

body.text: The concepts look obvious, but half of practical problems rest on them — from navigation to service reachability.

slides.title: Connected components
slides.sub: When a graph falls apart into islands
slides.main: In a connected graph you can get from any vertex to any other.

captions: A graph can fall apart into pieces
A connected graph: from any vertex you can reach any other
If there are several pieces, each is called a connected component: an island with no bridges to the rest
In a social network the components are communities with no mutual acquaintances
In dependencies a component is a group of packages that are installed and removed only together
Finding these islands is the first utilitarian problem about graphs, we will solve it in the next chapter

body.text: In a social network the components are communities with no mutual acquaintances; in dependencies — packages that are installed and removed only together. Finding these islands is the task of the next chapter.

slides.title: Three graphs from life
slides.main: Weights do not change the structure of a graph — to the question "how to get there" is added "at what cost".

captions: Let's reinforce this with three examples that you see every day
The browser's DOM tree is a directed graph, almost a tree: a node has one parent and any number of children
Package dependencies — an edge "is needed to work"; the manager will show a cycle in it as an error
A route map is a weighted graph: the edges carry minutes or dollars, a navigator looks for the minimal sum
Weights do not change the structure of a graph, but they add to "how to get there" the question "at what cost"

frames.text: a → b → c → a: a cycle — a manager error
minimal sum: A → C → D → E

body.text: A navigator looks for the path with the minimal sum of weights — this is how a weighted graph turns "how to get there" into "how to get there cheaper".

slides.title: The adjacency matrix
slides.sub: An n × n table: a one at the intersection means there is an edge
slides.main: Checking a specific edge is a constant: we looked into a cell and found out.

captions: How do you lay a graph out in memory?
The adjacency matrix: rows and columns are vertices, a one at the intersection means "there is an edge"
Checking whether there is an edge between two vertices is a constant: we look into a cell
Extreme simplicity: an ordinary two-dimensional array with no additional structures
For dense graphs, where there are many edges, the matrix is an honest choice

body.text: Plus extreme simplicity: a two-dimensional array with no structures at all. For dense graphs, where there are many edges, it is an honest choice.

slides.title: Adjacency lists
slides.sub: For each vertex — a list of its neighbors
slides.main: For sparse graphs lists are a radical saving of memory.

captions: The second way is adjacency lists: for each vertex we store the list of its neighbors
For sparse graphs, where there are incomparably fewer edges than possible pairs, this is a radical saving
A social network with a billion users: in a matrix — a quintillion cells, in lists — about 2 · 10¹¹ entries
The price: to find out whether two vertices are friends, you have to scan a list of neighbors
But the main traversal operation — "list the neighbors" — is done without fiddling with empty cells

frames.text: on average a person has a couple of hundred friends

body.text: The price: "are these two friends?" — you have to scan a list. But the main traversal operation — "list the neighbors" — is done without fiddling with empty cells.

slides.title: Matrix or lists
slides.sub: The choice comes down to two questions
slides.main: Real graphs are sparse and have to be walked continuously — practice is almost always on the side of lists.

captions: Let's reduce the choice to two questions
Is the graph dense or sparse? A matrix always eats V², lists take space proportional to the number of edges
Which operation is hot? Frequent edge checks — a matrix; constant iteration over neighbors — lists
Practice is almost always on the side of lists: real graphs are sparse and have to be walked continuously
A matrix wins in niches: small dense graphs and point checks

frames.text: in a sparse graph there are far fewer edges than V²

body.text: A matrix wins in niches: small dense graphs and point checks.

slides.title: Degrees in a digraph
slides.main: Each arrow leaves once and enters once — so both sums equal the number of edges.

captions: The directed versions of the concepts
The degree splits into the out-degree — how many arrows leave — and the in-degree — how many enter
The sum of the out-degrees equals the number of edges, and so does the sum of the in-degrees — an arrow leaves once and enters once
A popular page has a huge in-degree, its out-degree may be zero
Counting incoming arrows once gave birth to entire search engines

frames.text: the more links to a page — the more important it is

body.text: Once upon a time it was counting incoming arrows — who deserves how many links — that gave birth to entire search engines.

slides.title: Cycles and topological order
slides.sub: In dependencies a cycle is a synonym for trouble
slides.main: A graph without cycles is arranged so that every arrow leads from an earlier vertex to a later one.

captions: Separately — cycles in directed graphs: in dependencies they are a synonym for trouble
If a requires b, b requires c, and c requires a, none can be installed first: no order exists
A graph without cycles lets you arrange the vertices so that every arrow leads from early to late — a topological order
Checking for cycles and building the order are problems we will reach in a chapter's time

frames.text: where to start? — there is no correct order

body.text: This is exactly the order the package manager builds before installing. Checking for cycles and building the order are problems of the chapter on traversals.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: A graph is vertices and edges; everything else is derived questions about links.

captions: Summing up the chapter
A graph is vertices and edges: the most economical model for everything where links matter
Edges can be directed or not; the sum of degrees always equals twice the number of edges
A path, a cycle and connectivity describe reachability; a cycle in dependencies — no correct order
The easiest way to store a graph is adjacency lists for a sparse world and a matrix for a dense one
Next — we will learn to walk along graphs: depth, breadth, trees and the bridges of Königsberg

body.text: The next chapter is walking along graphs: depth, breadth, trees and the bridges of Königsberg.
